title: ts-bign npm Polymarket wallet stealer
synopsis: ts-bign 1.2.8 was one of the malicious npm packages embedded in a fake Polymarket trading bot hosted under the hijacked dev-protocol GitHub organization. The package posed as numeric-library plumbing but pulled in levex-refa, a transitive file stealer that searched for environment files, Solana keypairs, and trading-bot configuration, then exfiltrated them with local user and IP metadata. The case is historically useful because the scam bot still called real Polymarket APIs, making the theft path look like a functional trading tool.

title: big-nunber npm SSH backdoor installer
synopsis: big-nunber 5.0.2 was embedded in the same fake Polymarket trading bot hosted under the hijacked dev-protocol GitHub organization. It typosquatted bignumber.js but depended on lint-builder, which ran during npm install and at runtime to fetch instructions, steal files, fingerprint the host, and set up SSH access by taking ownership of ~/.ssh and opening port 22. The package combined credential theft with remote-access preparation while the bot continued to appear operational.

title: Trivy Repository Takeover via hackerbot-claw
synopsis: The hackerbot-claw account exploited a pull_request_target workflow in aquasecurity/trivy to run untrusted fork code with repository privileges. The stolen token was used to push directly to the repository, vandalize the README, temporarily privatize and rename the project, replace it with an empty repository, delete release assets from v0.27.0 through v0.69.1, and publish a suspicious Trivy VS Code extension artifact. Aqua restored the repository, revoked publishing tokens, removed the vulnerable workflow, and republished v0.69.2 while rebuilding release assets.

title: Glassworm Unicode Attack on reworm repo
synopsis: The Glassworm threat actor compromised the pedronauck/reworm GitHub repository and blended malicious code into realistic-looking commits. Invisible PUA Unicode characters hid the payload from casual review, making the repository appear ordinary while its source carried credential-stealing logic beneath the text.

title: kubernetes-el Emacs package repository compromise
synopsis: An attacker exploited a Pwn Request flaw in kubernetes-el's GitHub Actions workflow: pull_request_target ran with target-repository privileges and then checked out attacker-controlled PR code. The payload stole repository tokens and secrets, then used the token to push directly to master as github-actions[bot], deface the README, replace kubernetes.el with a destructive command that would run when loaded, and delete most repository files. MELPA removed the package and Emacsmirror updates were blocked, limiting downstream distribution.

title: ForceMemo GitHub Python repository force-push campaign
synopsis: ForceMemo was a GitHub account-takeover campaign that force-pushed similar malware into hundreds of Python repositories across Django apps, ML research, Streamlit dashboards, Flask APIs, and projects installed directly from GitHub. The attacker preserved legitimate commit authorship and messages while appending an obfuscated Python loader to common entry points. The malware used the shared marker lzcdrtfxyqiplpd, avoided Russian/CIS systems, and pulled encrypted follow-on instructions through a Solana memo wallet. This grouped record captures the campaign because the affected set was a moving GitHub code-search population rather than a stable package list.

title: Glassworm Unicode Attack on miso-client
synopsis: The Glassworm threat actor published a malicious version of @aifabrix/miso-client using invisible Unicode malware. The payload used PUA (Private Use Area) Unicode characters to hide the malicious script, which executed a second-stage payload (often delivered via Solana) to steal tokens and exfiltrate secrets.

title: Glassworm Unicode Attack on quartz-markdown-editor
synopsis: The Glassworm threat actor published a malicious version of the quartz.quartz-markdown-editor VS Code extension. Its payload was concealed with invisible PUA Unicode characters, hiding credential-theft logic in plain source view while the extension worked as a quiet collector of authentication tokens and secrets.

title: Glassworm Unicode Attack on watercrawl-mcp
synopsis: The Glassworm threat actor published malicious versions of @iflow-mcp/watercrawl-watercrawl-mcp with payloads hidden by invisible Unicode characters. The package kept the shape of a normal MCP dependency while concealed code executed credential stealers, letting source text itself become camouflage for supply-chain intrusion.

title: bittensor-wallet PyPI Private Key Exfiltration Backdoor
synopsis: A registry-only malicious release of bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 was uploaded to PyPI and later yanked. The backdoor was compiled into the Rust wallet code so wallet decryption paths exposed coldkey and hotkey material directly to the payload. It used sandbox checks, encrypted stolen key data with an attacker public key, deduplicated repeated unlocks, and exfiltrated through HTTPS, DNS lookups, and DNS tunneling. The release also removed bundled artifact-attestation workflow steps, making it harder to compare the PyPI artifact against the legitimate source release.

title: react-native-international-phone-number npm account takeover
synopsis: An attacker controlling the astroonauta npm account published malicious react-native-international-phone-number releases without matching GitHub releases, tags, or workflow runs. Aikido reported 0.11.8 was published on March 16, 2026 at 10:49:29 UTC with the same preinstall install.js loader used minutes later in react-native-country-select. Later releases hid the same malware behind a dependency chain through @agnoliaarisian7180/string-argv and @usebioerhold8733/s-format. The staged chain used Solana and Google Calendar indirection to deliver a Windows credential and wallet stealer.
story:
The first malicious react-native-international-phone-number release landed at 10:49:29 UTC on March 16, 2026. It added a preinstall hook that ran node install.js, while the prior adjacent 0.11.7 release did not include that hook. Aikido noted that 0.11.8 still depended on the clean react-native-country-select 0.3.9, which means this package was directly backdoored rather than merely poisoned by its dependency.

The loader followed the same staged path as the companion package. It queried Solana RPC for a memo, decoded a link, fetched a second stage, and decrypted a third-stage payload. The third stage used a Google Calendar URL to recover another slug, then requested more content from the same attacker-controlled IP address.

The recovered payload targeted Windows developer systems. It established persistence through schtasks and the HKCU Run key, wrote an init.json state file, downloaded Node.js runtimes, walked browser and wallet storage, collected npm and GitHub credentials, and posted the archive to attacker infrastructure. After disclosure, the same npm account was used in later releases that moved the delivery into a transitive dependency chain.

title: react-native-country-select npm account takeover
synopsis: The astroonauta npm account takeover also compromised react-native-country-select, a direct dependency of react-native-international-phone-number. Aikido reported 0.3.91 was published on March 16, 2026 at 10:54:18 UTC with a new preinstall hook and byte-identical install.js loader. After deprecation, the attacker retained access and republished through a transitive dependency chain ending in @usebioerhold8733/s-format. The malware used Solana and Google Calendar indirection to deliver a Windows credential and wallet stealer with persistence.
story:
The first react-native-country-select payload was small at the package boundary and large after execution. Version 0.3.91 added a preinstall hook that ran node install.js before npm finished the install. Aikido found the adjacent 0.3.9 release clean, making the change narrow and easy to describe: one new loader file and one lifecycle hook.

The loader reached to Solana RPC, recovered a transaction memo, decoded a URL, and fetched a second stage. The recovered chain continued through AES-decrypted JavaScript and a Google Calendar URL used as another indirection point before fetching more content from attacker infrastructure. The same install.js loader hash appeared in both React Native packages compromised that morning.

The later payload was Windows-focused theft code, not a harmless beacon. It set persistence with schtasks and an HKCU Run key, wrote an init.json guard, downloaded Node.js runtimes into AppData, walked browser profile and wallet storage, killed browser processes, stole npm and GitHub credentials, and exfiltrated collected archives. StepSecurity later tracked the attacker returning with additional releases that hid delivery behind transitive dependencies.
references: Malicious npm Releases Found in Popular React Native Packages - 130K Monthly Downloads Compromised <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-npm-releases-found-in-popular-react-native-packages---130k-monthly-downloads-compromised>, Malicious release report for react-native-country-select <https://github.com/AstrOOnauta/react-native-country-select/issues/11>, Glassworm Strikes Popular React Native Phone Number Packages <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-strikes-react-packages-phone-numbers>

title: Trivy v0.69.4 Release and Action Compromise
synopsis: After incomplete containment of the February Trivy takeover, compromised credentials were used to publish malicious Trivy v0.69.4 artifacts, force-push most trivy-action version tags, and replace setup-trivy tags with credential-stealing commits. The payloads read GitHub Actions runner memory and process environments, collected developer and cloud secrets, encrypted the data, and exfiltrated to the typosquatted domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org or fallback public tpcp-docs repositories. Compromised Docker Hub images followed on March 22. Aqua deleted affected tags, released fixed action versions, and published GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 / CVE-2026-33634.
story:
The second Trivy compromise was a containment failure with a long tail. After the February takeover, attackers still had usable access. On March 19, 2026, they used compromised credentials to publish Trivy v0.69.4 artifacts and to change action tags that existing CI/CD workflows already trusted.

The delivery path was not one file. It included the Trivy release, `trivy-action`, `setup-trivy`, and later Docker Hub images for 0.69.4, 0.69.5, and 0.69.6. Many workflows referenced mutable action tags instead of pinned commits, so force-pushed tags changed code under stable-looking configuration.

The payload read GitHub Actions runner memory and process environments, collected developer and cloud secrets, encrypted the archive, and tried to exfiltrate it to `scan.aquasecurtiy.org` or fallback public repositories. Trivy was valuable to the attacker because it already ran where secrets live: inside build and deployment pipelines.

The Register reported Mandiant's estimate of more than 1,000 impacted SaaS environments, with researchers warning that the number could grow. Aqua removed affected tags, released fixed action versions, and published GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23. The incident then bled into adjacent tools, including LiteLLM, through secrets stolen from CI/CD.

title: @opengov/form-builder CanisterWorm npm Backdoor
synopsis: TeamPCP's CanisterWorm campaign backdoored @opengov/form-builder 0.12.3 after npm publishing credentials were stolen through the second Trivy compromise. The malicious release added a postinstall payload that installed a persistent Python implant and polled an Internet Computer canister C2. The worm harvested npm publishing tokens, enumerated packages the victim could publish, bumped patch versions, injected the same payload, and republished with the latest tag. Follow-on capability included Kubernetes DaemonSet deployment that varied by geolocation and cluster context.

title: LiteLLM PyPI Credential Stealer and Kubernetes Backdoor
synopsis: TeamPCP compromised LiteLLM PyPI releases 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 with a credential-stealing payload that evolved from a proxy-module trigger to a wheel-level .pth file executed by Python at interpreter startup. The malware harvested environment, SSH, cloud, Kubernetes, package-manager, CI/CD, and wallet secrets, encrypted the archive with a TeamPCP RSA/AES scheme, and exfiltrated it as tpcp.tar.gz. It also attempted user-level persistence and, where Kubernetes permissions allowed, deployed privileged pods to backdoor cluster nodes. The incident is historically important as a stealthy Python-packaging abuse case where the second release executed even when LiteLLM itself was never imported.
story:
LiteLLM was a downstream hit from the Trivy compromise. According to LiteLLM maintainers, a bad Trivy scanner ran in the project's CI/CD pipeline and exposed the PyPI publishing token. The attacker used that token to publish LiteLLM 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 to PyPI.

The delivery path was direct Python package installation. The Register and LiteLLM maintainers identified `litellm_init.pth` in the compromised packages; Python processes `.pth` files at interpreter startup, so version 1.82.8 could execute before an application imported LiteLLM. The official LiteLLM Proxy Docker path was reported not impacted because it pinned dependencies and did not use the compromised PyPI packages.

The payload collected environment, SSH, cloud, Kubernetes, package-manager, CI/CD, and wallet secrets. It encrypted the archive using the TeamPCP RSA/AES pattern and wrote the stolen material as `tpcp.tar.gz`. Where Kubernetes permissions allowed, the malware also attempted privileged pod deployment for node access.

BerriAI removed the affected PyPI releases, deleted publishing tokens, rotated maintainer accounts, paused new releases, and engaged Mandiant while reviewing repositories and CI/CD. PyPA's advisory told anyone who installed and ran the affected package to assume credentials available to the LiteLLM environment were exposed and rotate them from clean systems.

title: IoliteLabs VS Code Solidity Extensions Backdoor
synopsis: A dormant IoliteLabs Visual Studio Marketplace publisher account was used to update three Solidity extensions to version 0.1.8 after nearly eight years of inactivity, with no matching source repository commits. The VSIX packages replaced the original language-server behavior with startup activation and hid the backdoor in a bundled copy of the pako dependency. The payload delivered Windows and macOS backdoors with persistence and exfiltration behavior; the Linux extension loaded the tampered dependency but did not contain an active Linux execution branch. The incident shows how dormant publisher accounts and vendored dependencies can hide malicious extension code away from the declared entry point.

title: Telnyx PyPI WAV Steganography Credential Stealer
synopsis: TeamPCP compromised Telnyx Python SDK releases 4.87.1 and 4.87.2 by adding import-time malware to the PyPI artifacts. The payload hid a second-stage credential stealer inside WAV audio data, collected developer, cloud, package-manager, and wallet secrets, encrypted them with the same TeamPCP RSA/AES scheme seen in LiteLLM, and exfiltrated them as tpcp.tar.gz. Version 4.87.2 also repaired a Windows branch intended to decode and persist a PE backdoor. The case stands out for using audio steganography inside a legitimate communications SDK package.

title: Axios npm Account Takeover and RAT
synopsis: A compromised axios maintainer account published malicious npm versions 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 on March 31, 2026. Both releases injected plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, whose install path delivered a multi-platform RAT and exposed machines that installed the brief releases. The package versions were live for about three hours before removal; affected systems were advised to remove the dependency and rotate secrets.
story:
The axios compromise was short, but it sat on a very large dependency graph. On March 31, 2026, an attacker used the lead maintainer's npm access to publish axios 1.14.1 and 0.30.4. The project later described the entry point as a compromised maintainer machine reached through targeted social engineering and RAT malware.

The malicious axios releases did not need to rewrite the library's public API. They added a dependency on plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, moving the payload into dependency resolution and install-time execution. A normal fresh install during the window could pull the poisoned axios version, then pull the malicious helper package from npm.

The payload was a remote access trojan for macOS, Windows, and Linux. The postmortem told affected users to inspect lockfiles for axios 1.14.1, axios 0.30.4, or plain-crypto-js, remove the malicious dependency, check for traffic to sfrclak[.]com or 142.11.206.73 on port 8000, and rotate every secret available to the affected machine or CI runner.

The timeline was measured in hours: axios 1.14.1 appeared at 00:21 UTC, axios 0.30.4 around 01:00 UTC, community detections followed almost immediately, and npm removed the malicious axios versions by 03:15 UTC. The project response moved toward immutable releases, OIDC publishing, stronger GitHub Actions hygiene, and a release process less dependent on one personal account.
references: Five Supply Chain Attacks in Twelve Days <https://blog.dreamfactory.com/five-supply-chain-attacks-in-twelve-days-how-march-2026-broke-open-source-trust-and-what-comes-next>, Axios Supply Chain Attack Reaches OpenAI macOS Signing Pipeline, Forces Certificate Rotation <https://socket.dev/blog/axios-supply-chain-attack-reaches-openai-macos-signing-pipeline-forces-certificate-rotation>, Post Mortem: axios npm supply chain compromise <https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/10636>

title: VeloraDEX SDK npm macOS Backdoor
synopsis: A registry-only malicious release of @velora-dex/sdk 9.4.1 was published to npm with no matching source commit. Instead of using an install hook, the attacker prepended code to the package entry point so importing the SDK downloaded and installed a macOS backdoor with launchctl persistence. The change was limited to package metadata and dist/index.js compared with the clean 9.4.0 tarball, making --ignore-scripts ineffective because execution moved from install time to first runtime import.

title: pgserve npm CanisterSprawl credential stealer
synopsis: On April 21, 2026, malicious pgserve npm versions 1.1.11, 1.1.12, and 1.1.13 added a postinstall loader that harvested developer and CI secrets, encrypted them with RSA-4096 and AES-256, and exfiltrated to an Internet Computer Protocol canister. The payload could propagate through npm publish tokens and PyPI tokens, turning an embedded PostgreSQL development package into a cross-ecosystem credential theft worm.
story:
pgserve was a small, convenient development dependency: an embedded PostgreSQL server meant to drop into Node.js projects with little ceremony. The malicious versions changed that trust boundary at install time. Versions 1.1.11, 1.1.12, and 1.1.13 were published to npm on April 21, 2026 without matching upstream git tags.

The package change was blunt and effective. Compared with the last legitimate release, 1.1.10, the malicious tarballs added scripts/check-env.js and scripts/public.pem, then wired package.json to run a postinstall command. The command ended with `|| true`, so an error in the malware would not break the install or warn the developer with a failed dependency.

The injected script harvested environment variables, package-manager tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials, Kubernetes and database material, crypto wallets, and browser password stores. Before transmission, it used a hybrid RSA-4096 and AES-256 scheme, then exfiltrated primarily to an Internet Computer Protocol canister and secondarily to a webhook if the right environment key was present.

The propagation logic made this more than a theft implant. If it found an npm publish token, it could enumerate packages the victim could publish, copy its loader and public key into each package, bump versions, and publish again. If it found a PyPI token, it attempted Python-package infection using .pth execution, crossing from npm into Python packaging.

title: Bitwarden CLI Compromise (Shai-Hulud V3)
synopsis: The official Bitwarden CLI npm package (@bitwarden/cli) version 2026.4.0 was compromised during the broader Checkmarx/TeamPCP supply-chain campaign after attackers abused a GitHub Actions path in Bitwarden's CI/CD pipeline. The malicious package included a bw1.js payload that shared infrastructure with the Checkmarx campaign, harvested GitHub, npm, cloud, SSH, environment, Claude, and MCP credentials, exfiltrated to audit.checkmarx.cx and GitHub commit-based dead drops, and attempted npm/GitHub supply-chain propagation with injected install hooks and workflow files.

title: Xinference PyPI Two-Stage Credential Stealer
synopsis: TeamPCP compromised three consecutive xinference PyPI releases, 2.6.0 through 2.6.2, by adding an import-time two-stage Python credential stealer to xinference/__init__.py. The attacker iterated the trigger across releases but kept the same core behavior: collect SSH keys, environment variables, cloud and Kubernetes credentials, package-manager tokens, CI/CD files, shell history, and wallet material, then archive and exfiltrate the results to attacker infrastructure. The incident is notable for its rapid multi-version refinement and for sharing TeamPCP markers and injection patterns with the LiteLLM and Telnyx compromises.

title: elementary-data PyPI and GHCR Forged Release
synopsis: An attacker exploited a GitHub Actions script-injection flaw in elementary-data's issue-update workflow to forge release state, tag v0.23.3 at an orphan commit, and dispatch the legitimate release pipeline. That pipeline published elementary-data==0.23.3 to PyPI and pushed compromised GHCR images tagged 0.23.3 and latest. The artifacts used a Python .pth file to execute at interpreter startup, unpack a multi-stage credential stealer, collect local, cloud, container, Kubernetes, package-manager, wallet, and system secrets, and exfiltrate them as trin.tar.gz.

title: SAP CAP Packages Mini Shai-Hulud
synopsis: Mini Shai-Hulud compromised SAP ecosystem npm packages mbt, @cap-js/sqlite, @cap-js/postgres, and @cap-js/db-service through two release paths: a stolen static npm token for mbt and an abused GitHub Actions OIDC publishing flow for cap-js/cds-dbs. The malicious releases ran a Bun-based credential stealer, exfiltrated encrypted secrets through attacker-created GitHub repositories, added IDE persistence through Claude Code and VS Code hooks, injected repository-secret stealing workflows, and attempted propagation through stolen npm tokens.

title: Intercom PHP SDK Compromise (Mini Shai-Hulud)
synopsis: The Mini Shai-Hulud campaign expanded into the PHP ecosystem by compromising the official intercom/intercom-php package on Packagist. Attackers compromised a maintainer account to overwrite existing legitimate versions. The malicious code was converted into a Composer plugin to execute automatically during installation, downloading the Bun runtime to execute an obfuscated payload that exfiltrated GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials, and .env files to zero.masscan.cloud.

title: Intercom Node.js SDK Compromise (Mini Shai-Hulud)
synopsis: The Mini Shai-Hulud/TeamPCP campaign compromised the official intercom-client package on npm. The malicious 7.0.4 release was published on April 30, 2026 at 14:41 UTC via a hijacked GitHub Actions OIDC publishing pipeline and introduced a preinstall hook, setup.mjs loader, and 11.7 MB obfuscated router_runtime.js payload. The payload used Bun v1.3.13, daemonized itself, harvested GitHub, npm, AWS, GCP, Azure, private-key, and generic API credentials, exfiltrated via GitHub private repositories under victim accounts, and attempted worm-style propagation through stolen npm publishing tokens.

title: Lightning PyPI wheel bundled Shai-Hulud credential stealer
synopsis: The Mini Shai-Hulud campaign compromised the lightning PyPI package, with malicious versions 2.6.2 and 2.6.3 bundling a hidden _runtime directory. On import, the package started a daemon thread that downloaded the Bun JavaScript runtime from GitHub and executed an 11 MB obfuscated _runtime/router_runtime.js payload. StepSecurity reported credential theft, environment and cloud secret harvesting, GitHub API exfiltration through victim credentials, and npm tarball poisoning on the developer machine.

title: TanStack npm packages compromised by Mini Shai-Hulud
synopsis: TeamPCP's Mini Shai-Hulud worm compromised the TanStack Router release pipeline by chaining a pull_request_target "Pwn Request" pattern, GitHub Actions cache poisoning, and runtime extraction of a GitHub Actions OIDC trusted-publisher token from runner memory. On 2026-05-11, malicious @tanstack/* versions added root payload files and an optional GitHub dependency on @tanstack/setup at an orphan commit whose prepare script ran tanstack_runner.js with Bun. The payload harvested cloud, Kubernetes, Vault, GitHub, npm, SSH, and local secrets, exfiltrated through Session/Oxen, and attempted npm self-propagation.
story:
The TanStack wave made provenance uncomfortable. The attacker did not only steal a registry token and push a tarball by hand. According to the public postmortem and follow-on research, the release path was abused through GitHub Actions: a pull_request_target pattern, cache poisoning, and extraction of trusted-publishing material from the runner while the workflow still looked like official automation.

The npm packages carried a new root-level payload file, reported by Aikido as router_init.js, and added an optional dependency on @tanstack/setup from a GitHub commit in the TanStack router repository. That dependency had a prepare script that ran tanstack_runner.js with Bun and then exited nonzero. Because it was optional, the visible install failure could be treated as noise after the code had already run.

The payload was built for developer workstations and CI/CD runners. It searched for GitHub and npm tokens, GitHub Actions OIDC material, AWS credentials and metadata endpoints, Kubernetes service account files, Vault tokens, environment variables, local filesystem secrets, and SSH material. Exfiltration and staging followed the broader Mini Shai-Hulud pattern, including Session/Oxen infrastructure and GitHub-centered propagation logic.

TanStack is recorded separately because its package scope and release pipeline evidence are unusually clear. Aikido counted 83 TanStack package-version entries within a broader May 2026 wave of 373 malicious package-version entries across 169 npm package names. This record preserves the TanStack artifacts, while the campaign record carries the shifting cross-ecosystem count.

title: Mistral AI Python SDK backdoored on PyPI
synopsis: The mistralai Python package version 2.4.6 contained an import-time Linux backdoor in src/mistralai/client/__init__.py. The added code downloaded https://83.142.209.194/transformers.pyz with curl -k, saved it to /tmp/transformers.pyz, and executed it as a background Python process when users imported mistralai, guarded only by the MISTRAL_INIT environment variable and silently swallowing errors. JFrog later reported that the remote payload changed from TeamPCP attribution text into a Python credential stealer that harvested local, cloud, Kubernetes, Vault, password-manager, and developer-tooling secrets, exfiltrated encrypted data, and could install pgsql-monitor persistence with destructive second-stage behavior.

title: OpenSearch npm prereleases compromised
synopsis: The Mini Shai-Hulud campaign reached OpenSearch when four prerelease versions of the official @opensearch-project/opensearch npm package were published with malicious payloads. The advisory maps the release window to May 11, 2026 EDT, or May 12 UTC, and recommends immediate removal of affected prereleases. The impact followed the broader worm pattern, with install-time credential theft risk and potential propagation through stolen developer and publishing tokens.
